title: Preventing Defaults in Response to Deteriorating Bank Health: The Prompt Corrective Action Approach
abstract: ABSTRACT Prior research shows that borrowers are more likely to default when their banks are financially distressed, particularly where contract enforcement is weak. We examine whether regulatory intervention in the form of Prompt Corrective Action (PCA), which seeks to improve bank health through enhanced monitoring, reverses such defaults. To address this question, we exploit the bright‐line entry thresholds in India's PCA regime using a regression discontinuity framework. We first show that such defaults exist in India. Our main result is that PCA intervention significantly reduces such defaults. The result is robust to variation in methodology and alternative definitions of bank health. Our evidence suggests that PCA reduces such defaults by credibly signaling to borrowers the likely restoration of bank health and continuity of lending relationships. Its effectiveness was reinforced by an earlier regulatory reform that improved the timeliness of loan‐loss provisioning, enhancing the credibility of enforcement. Overall, our findings suggest that PCA, when underpinned by credible financial reporting, can serve as an effective policy tool to curb strategic defaults.

summary.oneLiner: India's Prompt Corrective Action regime for weak banks reduces borrower defaults, suggesting it signals restored bank health and lending continuity.
summary.overview: Prior research finds borrowers are more likely to default when their banks are in financial distress, especially where contracts are hard to enforce. Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) is a regulatory intervention meant to improve struggling banks' health through closer monitoring. The authors use a regression discontinuity design, which compares banks just above and just below the bright-line thresholds that trigger PCA entry, to isolate its effect. They find PCA significantly reduces these defaults, and suggest it works by credibly signalling that bank health will be restored and lending relationships will continue. An earlier reform that made loan-loss provisioning more timely made the enforcement more credible and reinforced PCA's effect.
summary.question: Does regulatory intervention through Prompt Corrective Action reverse the borrower defaults that tend to rise when banks are financially distressed?
summary.method: Regression discontinuity framework (a design that compares cases just on either side of a cutoff), exploiting the bright-line entry thresholds of India's PCA regime. The authors also report that results are robust to variation in methodology and to alternative definitions of bank health.
summary.data: Setting is India's PCA regime for banks. The sample, time period and data source are not stated in the available text.
findings: Such defaults exist in India, the authors first show, consistent with prior research that borrowers default more when their banks are distressed, particularly where contract enforcement is weak.
PCA intervention significantly reduces such defaults.
The result is robust to variation in methodology and to alternative definitions of bank health.
The evidence suggests PCA reduces such defaults by credibly signalling to borrowers the likely restoration of bank health and continuity of lending relationships.
An earlier regulatory reform that improved the timeliness of loan-loss provisioning reinforced PCA's effectiveness by enhancing the credibility of enforcement.
Overall, the findings suggest PCA, when underpinned by credible financial reporting, can serve as an effective policy tool to curb strategic defaults.
summary.whyItMatters: The authors suggest PCA, especially when backed by credible financial reporting, can be an effective policy tool for curbing strategic defaults. For bank regulators, this points to the value of intervention that signals recovery to borrowers, and of timely loan-loss provisioning in making enforcement credible.
